name: Knowledge
title: Knowledge | Amplifier Smart Tools
promise: Ask your documents a question. See the answer as a map.
description: Point it at papers, specs, policies, notes or code and it builds a knowledge graph: concepts and typed relations, each with the passage it came from, a confidence and the dates it held. Ask in plain words and it answers in the form that fits the question: a timeline of what changed and what replaced it, an argument with the quotes for and against a claim, the steps between two ideas, a matrix of what is missing, a rhythm of when each topic was written about, or the map. When a question is unclear, it asks you instead of guessing.
alt: A short cut of the demos, all from real public material: Python's typing PEPs as a timeline of a replaced plan, a contested claim about emergent abilities as an argument with its quotes, US federal AI policy as a timeline of what applied on 2024-12-01, one graph shown six ways, the tool asking back when a question is vague, four agents building a graph live, and the commands an agent runs.
caption: A minute of what it does, on real public material: Python PEPs, arXiv abstracts and US federal policy.
flow_title: Read it. Ask it. See the answer in the right form.
flow_intro: Start from material you already have. The graph keeps every claim with its source and its dates, so you can follow a line of reasoning, check a claim, or see what applied on a given day, instead of searching for keywords.
steps: knowledge ingest ./docs has a model extract concepts and typed relations, each tied to the passage it came from. Inside an agent, --method agent hands the agent the passages instead, so no key is billed. --method cooccurrence builds a word network with no model at all.

knowledge visualize --for "what replaced M-24-10?" opens the form that answers it: a timeline for what changed, an argument for whether a claim holds, steps for how two ideas connect, a matrix for what is missing, a rhythm for when things were written, or the map. Every view file has all six as tabs. If the question is unclear, it asks which you meant, with the command for each answer.
Check it, and find what's missing.

evidence shows each supporting and contradicting relation with its quote. timeline and --as-of show what was believed on any date and what replaced it. gaps finds topics that should be linked but barely are: usually where the next question is.
details: Nothing is forgotten, nothing is overwritten.
Every relation has the dates it held. supersede closes one in favour of a newer one, a changed file closes its old claims, and --as-of shows the graph as it was on any day.
Agents write through add and relate with their name on every relation. The change log records who did what, and serve shows it live. Over MCP, the same capabilities are tools for any host.
One self-contained page with no outside requests. Export an Obsidian vault with wikilinks, topic notes, a gaps note and a Canvas map, or GraphML for Gephi, Cytoscape JSON and CSV.
prompt: Build a knowledge graph of ./docs and show me what replaced what. Use the knowledge tool: read knowledge --help, run knowledge ingest ./docs --method agent --graph docs --json, extract the relations from each passage yourself, load them with knowledge add, then open knowledge visualize --for "what changed over time?" --graph docs --open. If it asks a question back, ask me.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 or later, no other dependencies. Graphs are single SQLite files in your data folder; views are single HTML files that open offline.
model_note: ingest (default method), ask, report, questions and reconcile use a model: your host's own (through --complete-cmd or MCP), Anthropic, OpenAI or a local Ollama model. Inside Claude Code, Codex or Amplifier they stop and name the deterministic route instead of billing a key. Everything else needs no model.

capability_demos.title: A timeline of a plan that never shipped, and what replaced it.
capability_demos.description: Ten real Python Enhancement Proposals on type hints, including four versions of PEP 563. Ask "What replaced PEP 563's plan to make stringized annotations the default?" and it answers with a timeline. The plan moved from Python 4.0 (2017) to 3.10 (2020) and was put on hold for PEP 649 (2021); the PEP now says it "never became the default behaviour". Replaced plans are hatched, with an arrow to what replaced them: deferred evaluation in PEP 649 and PEP 749. Click any bar for its quote.
capability_demos.alt: A timeline of Python annotation plans: hatched bars for plans that were replaced, arrows to deferred evaluation, a selected relation with its quote.
capability_demos.caption: Screen recording. Public-domain PEP text from python/peps, relations extracted by an agent.

capability_demos.title: An argument: the claim, the quotes against it, the quotes for it.
capability_demos.description: Eight arXiv abstracts on scaling laws and emergent abilities (arXiv metadata is CC0). Ask "What contradicts the claim that emergent abilities appear suddenly and unpredictably?" and it answers with an argument. Wei et al. (2022) say such abilities "cannot be predicted simply by extrapolating" smaller models; Schaeffer et al. (2023) give evidence that they "evaporate with different metrics or with better statistics". Every card carries its quote and source. The same file shows the compute-optimal debate from Kaplan to Chinchilla as a timeline.
capability_demos.alt: An argument view: the emergence claim on top, four quote cards against it and two for it, one quote expanded.
capability_demos.caption: Screen recording. Abstracts from arXiv (CC0), relations extracted by an agent.
capability_demos.link_text: Open: what contradicts the emergence claim?

capability_demos.eyebrow: For policy, legal and operations work
capability_demos.title: What agencies had to do on a given day, and what applies now.
capability_demos.description: Seven US federal documents on agency use of AI, from Executive Order 14110 (2023) to OMB memos M-25-21 and M-25-22 (2025), all public domain. Ask "What did agencies have to do as of 2024-12-01?" and it answers with a timeline marked at that date: requirements in force then, such as M-24-10's December 1, 2024 deadline for minimum practices, and the ones that replaced them after M-25-21 "rescinds and replaces" it. Filled bars still hold; hatched bars ended, with the sentence that ended them.
capability_demos.alt: A timeline of US federal AI policy marked 'as of 2024-12-01': hatched bars for rescinded requirements, filled bars for what still holds, a selected requirement in the side panel.
capability_demos.caption: Screen recording. US government works (public domain), relations extracted by an agent.

capability_demos.title: The question picks the form. The tabs show the rest.
capability_demos.description: Data, knowledge and wisdom need different pictures. Map: the network of concepts and relations. Timeline: what held when, and what replaced it. Argument: a claim with the quotes for and against. Steps: the chain between two ideas, each with its sentence. Matrix: topics against topics, links observed against expected, gaps outlined. Rhythm: topics against time. One self-contained file, no outside requests.
capability_demos.alt: The Python typing graph cycling through its six tabs: map, timeline, argument, steps, matrix and rhythm.
capability_demos.caption: Screen recording. Public-domain PEP text.

capability_demos.title: A vague question gets a question back.
capability_demos.description: Ask "What about scaling?" and the tool does not pick a view for you. It names what it could not tell, offers the concepts you might mean, and gives the exact command for each answer (exit 1, needs_clarification). An agent puts the question to you and runs the one you choose. It never prompts by itself, so scripts and agents never hang.
capability_demos.alt: A terminal: knowledge visualize --for "What about scaling?" returns a question and five choices; the chosen command then opens its view.
capability_demos.caption: Real output from the scaling-laws graph, replayed as typed.

capability_demos.title: What's missing, as a matrix.
capability_demos.description: Twenty real documents from Microsoft's Amplifier docs and the smart-tools spec, read by four agents into 313 concepts and 613 relations. The matrix sets every topic against every other: links observed against links expected for their size. Outlined cells are gaps. The biggest is real: the smart-tools world (cli, smart tool, manifest) barely touches the kernel world (kernel, mount plan, module). Click a gap for its bridge candidates.
capability_demos.alt: A topic matrix of the Amplifier docs: warm cells for fewer links than expected, outlined gap cells, one selected with its bridge candidates.
capability_demos.caption: Screen recording. Microsoft's public Amplifier docs (MIT), relations extracted by agents.

capability_demos.title: Four agents built this graph, live.
capability_demos.description: Four Claude Code agents, a cartographer, an analyst, a skeptic and an archivist, each took 25 chunks of the docs and wrote what they found with knowledge add, at the same time, while knowledge serve was recorded. Nearly five minutes of real work, sped up. They checked each other's names as they went.
capability_demos.alt: The live view filling from empty as four agents write; a ticker shows each agent's relations as they land.
capability_demos.caption: Screen recording of real agents, sped up 6.5 times.

capability_demos.title: Plain commands, real answers, no key.
capability_demos.description: Inside Claude Code, Codex or Amplifier, the agent is the model. These commands need no credentials: the biggest gap, a path between two ideas, the contradictions, and numbered context ready to cite, all from the real Amplifier docs graph.
capability_demos.alt: A terminal running knowledge gaps, path, contradictions and context, with their output.
capability_demos.caption: Real output from the Amplifier docs graph, replayed as typed.

capability_demos.title: This repository's docs, as a word network.
capability_demos.description: ingest --method cooccurrence links words that appear near each other, the text-network way. No model, same result every time, and still topics, influence and gaps. Search for a word, then switch topics on and off.
capability_demos.alt: A dense word network of the tool's own documentation, coloured by topic; a search highlights graph and its neighbours.
capability_demos.caption: Screen recording. Built from this repository's README and docs.

install_options.title: Coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Amplifier
install_options.text: Install the knowledge tool from https://github.com/michaeljabbour/amplifier-smart-tool-visualizer by following its README, then run knowledge doctor

install_options.title: Any MCP host
install_options.note: Add it as a local stdio server. Model-backed tools return a task for the assistant, so the host's model does the thinking.

install_footnote: All examples are real public material with provenance: Python PEPs (public domain or CC0), arXiv abstracts (CC0), US federal documents (public domain), and Microsoft's Amplifier docs and history (MIT). Relations were extracted by agents through the tool's own agent route; every relation links to its quote.
